entries.text: Spring AI: Decision Models | Decision Extensions | Demo Applications often need to make decisions with a predefined set of outcomes: Is this message a jailbreak attempt? Which team should handle this support ticket? How helpful is this answer? A chat model can handle these tasks, but the application still has to turn its text reply into a boolean, an enum or a numeric score. Last year we used a chat model and recursive advisors to implement LLM-as-a-Judge. That is still a useful approach, particularly when an evaluation requires general knowledge, reasoning or a written explanation of what went wrong. For many classification and evaluation tasks, however, the input contains all the information needed to make the decision. Specialized decision models can perform these tasks at comparable accuracy, with considerably lower latency and cost, and they provide typed answers together with probability information. In an independent study, Jev came within three points of a frontier chat model on such tasks, at a median latency of 0.15 seconds and less than 1% of the cost. It fell behind where the verdict had to be derived, as in math, code and logic. Spring AI 2.1 adds a DecisionModel API for these decisions. It is not a Chat Model: a decision model works with predefined outcomes and returns typed answers with probabilities. That makes it a different programming abstraction, not only a faster model. entries.text: Hi, Spring fans! And Happy Thanksgiving to you, if you celebrate! I am VERY thankful for you! And today we've got an extra special episode! I'm joined by my friend and colleague and mentor Cora Iberkleid. What if AI isn’t just changing how we write code-but how we upgrade, patch, secure, and even trust it? In this conversation, we dive into the hidden complexity AI is creating in software development, why human judgment matters more than ever, and how deterministic tools like OpenRewrite and AppAdvisor are reshaping the future of safe, scalable upgrades. From supply chain security and SBOMs to the new reality of keeping software always releasable, this is a must-watch for anyone building in the age of AI.
entries.title: A Bootiful Podcast: Cora Iberkleid on AI, Microservices, and the Future of Software Upgrades

entries.summary: Spring AI: Tool Call Confirmation | Session Extensions | Demo A bank support agent can look up why a mortgage payment failed.
entries.text: Spring AI: Tool Call Confirmation | Session Extensions | Demo A bank support agent can look up why a mortgage payment failed. That is reading, and the model may do it on its own. Collecting the payment today moves money, and a person must approve it first. Asking "may I?" is the easy part. The hard part is the wait. The approver answers minutes or hours later, maybe on another instance of the application, maybe after a restart. Whatever the agent was doing must still be there when the answer comes. In Spring AI 2.0, approving a tool call meant user-controlled tool execution: you switch the tool loop off and run every round yourself. That is a lot to take over for one call. Spring AI 2.1 adds tool call confirmation: you mark a tool, and the loop runs the harmless tools as before and pauses only when the model asks for a marked one. The 2.1.0 GA announcement covered it in one paragraph. This post shows how it works, and how the new community project Spring AI Session Extensions keeps the pause in the session log, so that another process can resume it. Mark the tool The mark goes on the tool. Check out this scheduled livestream on youtube.com/@coffeesoftware and join the discussion: how are you using your favorite IDE(s) in the age of AI?
